{{Short description|Local ring in which Hensel's lemma holds}}
{{More footnotes needed|date=December 2024}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Henselian ring''' (or '''Hensel ring''') is a  [[local ring]] in which [[Hensel's lemma]] holds. They were introduced by {{harvtxt|Azumaya|1951}}, who named them after [[Kurt Hensel]]. Azumaya originally allowed Henselian rings to be [[non-commutative ring|non-commutative]], but most authors now restrict them to be [[commutative ring|commutative]].

Some standard references for Hensel rings are  {{harv|Nagata|1975|loc=Chapter VII}}, {{harv|Raynaud|1970}}, and {{harv|Grothendieck|1967|loc=Chapter 18}}.

==Definitions==
In this article [[ring (mathematics)|rings]] will be assumed to be commutative, though there is also a theory of non-commutative Henselian rings.

* A local ring ''R'' with [[maximal ideal]] ''m'' is called '''Henselian''' if  Hensel's lemma holds. This means that if ''P'' is a [[monic polynomial]] in ''R''[''x''], then any factorization of its image ''P'' in (''R''/''m'')[''x''] into a product of [[coprime polynomials|coprime]] monic polynomials  can be lifted to a factorization in ''R''[''x''].
* A local ring is Henselian if and only if every finite ring extension is a [[product of rings|product]] of local rings.
* A Henselian local ring is called '''strictly Henselian''' if its [[residue field]] is [[separable extension|separably closed]].
* By [[abuse of notation|abuse of terminology]], a '''[[field (mathematics)|field]]''' <math>K</math> with [[Valuation (algebra)|valuation]] <math>v</math> is said to be Henselian if its [[valuation ring]] is Henselian. That is the case if and only if <math>v</math> extends uniquely to every [[finite extension]] of <math>K</math> (resp. to every finite separable extension of <math>K</math>, resp. to <math>K^{alg}</math>, resp. to <math>K^{sep}</math>).
* A ring is called Henselian if it is a direct product of a finite number of Henselian local rings.

=== Properties ===

* Assume that <math>(K, v)</math> is a Henselian field. Then every [[algebraic extension]] of <math>K</math> is henselian (by the fourth definition above).
* If <math>(K, v)</math> is a Henselian field and <math>\alpha</math> is algebraic over <math>K</math>, then for every [[Conjugate element (field theory)|conjugate]] <math>\alpha'</math> of <math>\alpha</math> over <math>K</math>, <math>v(\alpha') = v(\alpha)</math>. This follows from the fourth definition, and from the fact that for every K-automorphism <math>\sigma</math> of <math>K^{alg}</math>, <math>v\circ \sigma</math> is an extension of <math>v|_K</math>. The converse of this assertion also holds, because for a [[normal field extension]] <math>L/K</math>, the extensions of <math>v</math> to <math>L</math> are known to be conjugated.<ref>A. J. Engler, A. Prestel, ''Valued fields'', Springer monographs of mathematics, 2005, thm. 3.2.15, p. 69.</ref>

==Henselian rings in algebraic geometry==
Henselian rings are the local rings with respect to the [[Nisnevich topology]] in the sense that if <math>R</math> is a Henselian local ring, and <math>\{U_i \to X\}</math> is a Nisnevich covering of <math>X = Spec(R)</math>, then one of the <math>U_i \to X</math> is an isomorphism. This should be compared to the fact that for any [[Zariski topology|Zariski]] open covering <math>\{U_i \to X\}</math> of the spectrum <math>X = Spec(R)</math> of a local ring <math>R</math>, one of the <math> U_i \to X </math> is an isomorphism. In fact, this property characterises Henselian rings, resp. local rings.

Likewise strict Henselian rings are the local rings of geometric points in the [[étale topology]].

==Henselization==
For any local ring ''A'' there is a universal Henselian ring ''B'' generated by ''A'', called the '''Henselization''' of ''A'', introduced by {{harvtxt|Nagata|1953}}, such that any [[local homomorphism]] from ''A'' to a Henselian ring can be extended uniquely to ''B''. The Henselization of ''A'' is unique [[up to]] unique [[isomorphism]]. The Henselization of ''A'' is an algebraic substitute for the [[completion of a ring|completion]] of ''A''. The Henselization of ''A'' has the same completion and residue field as ''A'' and is a [[flat module]] over ''A''.  If ''A'' is [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]], [[reduced ring|reduced]], normal, regular, or [[excellent ring|excellent]] then so is its Henselization. For example, the Henselization of the [[ring of polynomials]] ''k''[''x'',''y'',...] [[localization (commutative algebra)|localized]] at the point (0,0,...) is the ring of algebraic [[formal power series]] (the formal [[power series]] satisfying an algebraic equation). This can be thought of as the "algebraic" part of the completion.

Similarly there is a strictly Henselian ring generated by ''A'', called the '''strict Henselization''' of ''A''. The strict Henselization is not quite universal: it is unique, but only up to ''non-unique'' isomorphism. More precisely it depends on the choice of a separable algebraic closure of the residue field of ''A'', and [[automorphism]]s of this separable algebraic closure correspond to automorphisms of the corresponding strict Henselization. For example, a strict Henselization of the field of [[p-adic number|''p''-adic numbers]] is given by the maximal unramified extension, generated by all [[roots of unity]] of order prime to ''p''. It is not "universal" as it has [[trivial automorphism|non-trivial]] automorphisms.

==Examples==
*Every field is a Henselian local ring. (But not every field with valuation is "Henselian" in the sense of the fourth definition above.)
*Complete [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] local rings, such as the ring of [[p-adic integer|''p''-adic integers]] and rings of formal power series over a field, are Henselian.
*The rings of convergent power series over the [[real number|real]] or [[complex number]]s are Henselian.
*Rings of algebraic power series over a field are Henselian.
*A local ring that is [[integral element|integral]] over a Henselian ring is Henselian.
*The Henselization of a local ring is a Henselian local ring.
*Every [[quotient ring|quotient]] of a Henselian ring is Henselian.
*A ring ''A'' is Henselian if and only if the associated [[reduced ring]] ''A''<sub>red</sub> is Henselian (this is the quotient of ''A'' by the [[Nilradical of a ring|ideal of nilpotent elements]]).
*If ''A'' has only one [[prime ideal]] then it is Henselian since ''A''<sub>red</sub> is a field.
